notes.meaning: Balaam asks King Balak to build seven altars and provide seven bulls and seven rams for sacrifice. In the ancient world, the number seven symbolized completeness, and Balaam was using pagan customs to try to win God's favor. True worship never required building many altars at once, but God used this moment to display His own power.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars note that these multiple sacrifices were common in ancient pagan divination, where animal organs were examined to predict the future.

notes.meaning: Balak follows Balaam’s directions, and the two men offer a bull and a ram on each of the seven altars. In ancient kingdoms, rulers often carried out priestly duties alongside prophets. They hoped these costly offerings would persuade the God of Israel to let them curse His people.

Balaam tells Balak to stand waiting by his burnt offerings while he goes alone to a bare hilltop. As a seer, Balaam was looking for a quiet place where he could search for natural omens or receive a message from the Lord. He promised to report back everything God revealed to him.

God meets with Balaam, and Balaam quickly boasts about the seven altars and sacrifices he has prepared. Balaam thought his rituals had earned God’s attention and favor. God met him not because He approved of pagan rituals, but to protect Israel and accomplish His own purpose.

The Lord puts a specific message directly into Balaam’s mouth and commands him to go back and speak it to Balak. God took total control of this corrupt seer's speech, just as He had previously spoken through Balaam's donkey. Balaam was given no freedom to invent his own words.

Balaam returns and finds Balak waiting by the altars, surrounded by all the royal leaders of Moab. The king and his princes were eagerly waiting to hear a curse pronounced against their feared enemy. Instead, they were about to hear God's own unbreakable word.

Balaam begins to speak his prophetic message in formal, poetic language. He explains how Balak brought him from the eastern mountains of Aram to place a curse on the descendants of Jacob. He makes it clear from the start what the king hired him to do.

Balaam asks how he can possibly curse a people whom God Himself has not cursed. No magical spell or human desire has any power against the blessing and decree of the Almighty. Even though Balaam wanted Balak's reward, he had to admit that God's protection over Israel could not be broken.

Looking down from the rocky cliffs, Balaam sees Israel living as a distinct people, separate from all other nations. God set them apart with their own laws, worship, and divine protection so they would not be blended into the pagan world. Their unique standing came entirely from God choosing and caring for them.

Balaam marvels at Israel’s vast numbers, recalling God's promise to Abraham that his family would become as numerous as dust. He ends with a personal wish that he might die the peaceful, blessed death of God’s upright people. Sadly, Balaam wished for a righteous death without choosing to live a righteous life.

Balak is furious and asks Balaam what he has done, complaining that he hired him to curse his enemies but got only blessings instead. The king thought he could purchase a curse with wealth and sacrifices. He is stunned to find that his hired seer has completely ruined his plan.

Balaam defends himself by asking if he is not required to speak whatever the Lord puts into his mouth. He makes it sound like he is acting out of holy devotion, but in reality God forced him to speak the truth against his own desires. He could not alter a single word of God's message.

Balak urges Balaam to try a different location where he can see only the edge of Israel’s camp rather than the entire army. He believed that the full view of the huge camp had overwhelmed the seer, or that a change of viewpoint might bring better magic. The king hoped that cursing a smaller fraction of the people would finally succeed.

Balak leads Balaam to the ridge of Pisgah at the field of Zophim, a lookout used by watchmen. There they repeat the entire ritual, setting up seven altars and offering a bull and a ram on each one. Balak was willing to spend great wealth repeatedly in his vain attempt to bend God's will.

Balaam tells Balak to remain by his burnt offering while he goes aside to seek the Lord once more. Having met God earlier, Balaam was confident that the Lord would speak to him again. He still hoped that somehow a message favorable to the king might be given.

The Lord meets Balaam again and puts a new message directly into his mouth. God then instructs him to return to Balak and deliver the exact words he has been given. Once again, the sovereign God takes command of the seer's voice.

Balaam returns and finds Balak still waiting by the sacrifices alongside the Moabite princes. The anxious king immediately asks what the Lord had said. Balak knew Balaam was speaking for Jehovah, but he still foolishly hoped God might have changed His mind.

Balaam commands Balak to rise up and listen closely to what he is about to say. This call to attention shows that an urgent and weighty message from God is coming. Even a royal king must stand in respect and submit to the word of the Lord.

Balaam declares that God is not human, so He does not lie or change His mind. People often break their word because they are fickle, lack power, or discover new facts, but God always fulfills whatever He promises. Because God's character never wavers, Balak cannot bribe or persuade Him to abandon Israel.

differ.view: God's eternal decrees and His choice of His people never change, so texts speaking of God repenting only describe a change in how He acts toward men, not a change in His mind.

notes.meaning: Balaam explains that he received an absolute order to bless Israel, and because God has blessed them, no one can overturn it. The seer admits he has no power of his own to reverse what the Lord has decreed. When God sets His favor upon His people, no enemy can take it away.

The oracle announces that God sees no lasting wickedness or misery in Israel to justify destroying them. The Lord their God lives among them, and they celebrate Him with joyful shouts like a victorious king. Although the people were not sinless, God was faithful to His covenant and refused to abandon them to their enemies.

God is actively bringing Israel out of Egypt with overwhelming strength, like the horns of a powerful wild ox. Israel was no longer a weak, enslaved group of wanderers, but a mighty nation guarded by God’s power. Balak’s resistance was useless because fighting Israel meant fighting the Almighty God who led them.

Balaam confesses that spells and omens have no effect against Jacob, because God's people are fully protected from dark magic. Instead, people will look at Israel and wonder with awe at the great things God has done for them. God's mighty works for His people become a lasting witness to the entire world.

Israel is compared to a fierce lioness and a strong young lion rising up to hunt. Just like a lion does not rest until it has caught and consumed its prey, Israel will not stop until its enemies are defeated. This picture confirmed to Balak that the nation he feared would conquer the land ahead of them.

Balak cries out in desperation, telling Balaam that if he cannot curse Israel, he should at least keep completely silent and not bless them. The king was willing to settle for nothing rather than hear his enemy praised again. His frustration grew as every effort produced the exact opposite of what he wanted.

Balaam reminds Balak of his earlier warning that he could only do and say what the Lord commanded. Even though Balaam craved the king's riches, he was completely bound by God's overpowering hand. God can compel even an unwilling messenger to speak His truth.

Balak refuses to give up and asks Balaam to come with him to yet another mountaintop. He hopes that a new sacred spot might finally please God and allow a curse to be spoken. In his pagan thinking, the king imagined God's mind could be changed by switching locations.

Balak takes Balaam to the summit of Mount Peor, which looks out over the desert wasteland. This peak was a famous center for worshiping the local idol Baal-peor, and it stood close to Israel's encampment. Balak hoped this idol shrine would give him spiritual leverage against God's people.

For a third time, Balaam tells Balak to build seven altars and prepare seven bulls and seven rams. Balaam still hoped to gain Balak's promised wealth, so he was willing to repeat the elaborate ritual once again. Human persistence in ritual cannot alter what God has settled.

Balak obeys the seer once more and sacrifices a bull and a ram on each of the seven altars. The king spared no expense or effort, clinging to the faint hope of victory over Israel. Yet all his sacrifices were powerless against the unchangeable blessing of the Lord.
